## In brief

Lin et al. reveal BRAT1/CG7044 as a binding partner for the INTS11 endonuclease that behaves like a cytoplasmic chaperone and is required for Integrator function in the nucleus. UBE3D is also identified as a binding partner for the CPSF73 endonuclease in pre-mRNA 3 0 -end processing, with a similar mechanism of action.

## Cytoplasmic binding partners of the Integrator endonuclease INTS11 and its paralog CPSF73 are required for their nuclear function

Min-Han Lin, 1,5,6 Madeline K. Jensen, 2,3,6 Nathan D. Elrod, 3 Hsu-Feng Chu, 1 MaryClaire Haseley, 2 Alissa C. Beam, 2 Kai-Lieh Huang, 2,3 Wesley Chiang, 2 William K. Russell, 3 Kelsey Williams, 2,4 Christoph Pro ¨ schel, 2,4 Eric J. Wagner, 2,3,7, * and Liang Tong 1,7,8, *

## SUMMARY

INTS11 and CPSF73 are metal-dependent endonucleases for Integrator and pre-mRNA 3 0 -end processing, respectively. Here, we show that the INTS11 binding partner BRAT1/CG7044, a factor important for neuronal fitness, stabilizes INTS11 in the cytoplasm and is required for Integrator function in the nucleus. Loss of BRAT1 in neural organoids leads to transcriptomic disruption and precocious expression of neurogenesisdriving transcription factors. The structures of the human INTS9-INTS11-BRAT1 and Drosophila dIntS11CG7044 complexes reveal that the conserved C terminus of BRAT1/CG7044 is captured in the active site of INTS11, with a cysteine residue directly coordinating the metal ions. Inspired by these observations, we find that UBE3D is a binding partner for CPSF73, and UBE3D likely also uses a conserved cysteine residue to directly coordinate the active site metal ions. Our studies have revealed binding partners for INTS11 and CPSF73 that behave like cytoplasmic chaperones with a conserved impact on the nuclear functions of these enzymes.

## INTRODUCTION

Transcription termination is an obligatory event in the RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) life cycle (reviewed in Eaton and West 1 and Rodrı ´guez-Molina et al. 2 ). Multiple mechanisms exist to ensure transcription termination occurs robustly at the proper location. Near the 3 0 -ends of protein-coding genes, ''canonical termination'' is carried out by the cleavage and polyadenylation (CPA) machinery that simultaneously causes the removal of RNAPII from the DNA template, 2 while the replication-dependent histone pre-mRNA 3 0 -end processing machinery (U7 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle [snRNP]) produces a non-polyadenylated mRNA. 3 More recently, at the 5 0 -ends of protein-coding genes, it has been found that the Integrator complex (INT) is responsible for executing promoter-proximal termination, 4-10 attenuating transcription. Despite significant differences in the constituency between INT and the CPA machinery, common mechanistic themes are apparent. Both complexes incorporate phosphatase activities to reverse the effect of elongation stimulatory kinases (i.e., pTEFb) 6,11-14 and utilize RNA endonucleases to cleave nascent RNA, 4,7,9,15-19 which generates access points for exonucleases such as XRN2 20 to promote termination. Impairment of either enzymatic activities results in loss of efficient termination by INT 10 or the CPA machinery. 13

The role of INT in promoter-proximal termination has only recently been revealed. 21 INT is a 17-subunit protein complex associated with RNAPII that is crucial for 3 0 -end processing of snRNAs 22 and other noncoding RNAs, 23-26 as well as premature termination through cleavage of nascent mRNA transcripts on paused, promoter-proximal RNAPII. 4,5,21,27-29 Structural studies reveal that INT is composed of several modules, 21 including a backbone that contains INTS1/2/7/12 7,12,30 and a shoulder comprised of INTS5/8. 31,32 These two modules form a scaffold upon which two enzymatic factors associate: the Integrator phosphatase module containing PP2A/C/INTS6 6,11 and the

Integrator cleavage module (ICM) containing INTS4/9/11. 31,33,34 INTS9 and INTS11 are paralogs of CPSF100 and CPSF73 in the CPA machinery and the U7 snRNP, 35 with CPSF73 catalyzing the cleavage reaction in these machineries, 16,36,37 and INTS11 being the endonuclease for Integrator. 22 CPSF73 and INTS11 belong to the metallob -lactamase-associated CPSF, Artemis, SNM1/PSO2 ( b -CASP) family of nucleases, 38 and their active sites are between a metallob -lactamase and a b -CASP domain, with two metal ions critical for catalysis. CPSF73 and INTS11 exist in a closed, inactive conformation on their own. They transition to an open conformation for catalysis, with a deep canyon between the metallob -lactamase and b -CASP domains to bind the RNA substrate.

Integrator has also been reported to interact with other factors, including a collection of zinc finger proteins, 39,40 BRAT1, 41 WDR73, 42 and the SOSS complex. 43-45 BRAT1 (CG7044 in Drosophila ) was initially identified by its association with BRCA1 and ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), 46 and mutations of BRAT1 have been linked to several neurological diseases. 47,48 Loss of BRAT1 disrupts UsnRNA 3 0 -end processing and premature termination at nascent mRNAs, which indicates its expression is somehow required for INT function. 41 The neurological disruptions observed in BRAT1 patients have parallels with symptoms associated with variants of WDR73 and INT subunits, 42,49-51 suggesting a common requirement during neuronal differentiation.

We show here that BRAT1 and CG7044 are primarily cytoplasmic proteins distinct from the nuclear INT. Using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we determined the structures of Drosophila dIntS11-CG7044 and human INTS9-INTS11BRAT1 complexes. The structures reveal, unexpectedly, that the conserved C terminus of BRAT1/CG7044 is captured in the active site of INTS11, with INTS11 in a previously unobserved, ''semi-open'' state to accommodate this C terminus. Moreover, the conserved penultimate Cys residue is directly coordinated to the metal ions in the active site. BRAT1 engagement to the INTS11 active site is critical to INT function as mutations of the BRAT1 C terminus prevent rescue of INT loss of function in BRAT1 null cell lines. Further, loss of BRAT1 in neural organoids (NOs) leads to transcriptomic disruption and precocious expression of neurogenesis-driving transcription factors. Our observations with INTS11 inspired us to search for a similar partner for CPSF73. We found that UBE3D can form a stable complex with CPSF73, and a long segment on the surface of UBE3D likely extends into the CPSF73 active site, remarkably also with a conserved Cys residue likely directly coordinating the metal ions. These studies demonstrate the unexpected existence of cytoplasmic partners for INTS11 and CPSF73 that may share conserved features in their binding to the cognate endonucleases.

results.subtitle: ## BRAT1/CG7044 is a conserved, primarily cytoplasmic factor associated with INTS11
results.content:
Structural and biochemical analyses of Integrator have revealed its modular nature, 12,15,31,33,34,52 but little is known about the biochemical, structural, and physiological relevance of Integrator-associated factors such as BRAT1. 41 We generated total cell extracts from S2 cell lines stably expressing FLAG-tagged dIntS5, dIntS11, or empty vector as a control. As expected, using affinity purification followed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), we observed strong enrichment of all 17 Drosophila Integrator subunits in both FLAG-dIntS5 (Figure 1A) and FLAG-dIntS11 relative to control (Figure 1B). Interestingly, CG7044 was only observed in FLAG-dIntS11 purification (Figure 1B; Table S1). We extended this analysis to complexes associated with FLAG-dIntS1 or FLAG-dIntS8 and used LC-MS (Figure S1A; Table S1) and western blotting (Figure S1B) to confirm that CG7044 is only associated with dIntS11. Finally, we generated a reciprocal S2 cell line stably expressing FLAG-CG7044 and compared associated complexes to those observed from the purification of FLAG-dIntS1, FLAG-dIntS5, or control. Using western blot (Figure 1C) and LC-MS analysis (Figure S1C; Table S1), we found that CG7044 associates strongly with dIntS11 and, to a lesser extent, dIntS9, but no other Integrator subunits were observed.

BRAT1 was initially described as a mostly cytoplasmic protein capable of shuttling into the nucleus, 53 but this has yet to be assessed in the context of Integrator localization and function, which is thought to be nuclear. To address this, we first fractionated human HEK293T cells into nuclear and cytoplasmic extracts (Figure 1D). As expected, most Integrator subunits display predominantly nuclear localization except INTS11, which is observed in both compartments as consistent with previous reports. 54 By contrast, endogenous BRAT1 is primarily cytoplasmic, suggesting its function may be distinct from that of the nuclear Integrator. The prevalent cytoplasmic localization of BRAT1 was confirmed using indirect immunofluorescence (Figure S1D). Our observations on INTS11 and BRAT1 in human cells are conserved in Drosophila cells (Figure 1E).

Given the cellular localization of BRAT1/CG7044 and INTS11 within human and fly cells, we used proteomics analysis to identify associated proteins in either compartment. To that end, we affinity purified complexes from cytoplasmic or nuclear extracts from HEK293T and S2 cells stably expressing exogenous FLAGtagged INTS11, BRAT1/CG7044, or control. In the cytoplasm, human FLAG-INTS11 and FLAG-BRAT1 interact with each other, INTS9, and another Integrator-associated protein, WDR73 (Figure 1F; Table S1). In Drosophila , we found that FLAG-dIntS11 and FLAG-CG7044 also interact with each other

in the cytoplasm and a smaller amount of dIntS9 (Figure 1G; Table S1). Notably, no other protein was significantly enriched in the fly dIntS11-CG7044 complex, and no readily identifiable ortholog exists for WDR73, suggesting it may be a vertebratespecific interaction. In the nucleus, both human and fly FLAGINTS11 are observed to interact with the entire INT, several members of the pre-elongation complex, and BRAT1. On the contrary, FLAG-tagged BRAT1/CG7044 in the nucleus was still only associated with INTS9 and INTS11 (Figures 1F and 1G). Altogether, these results indicate that a distinct ''pool'' of INTS9 and INTS11 is associated with BRAT1/CG7044 primarily in the cytoplasm, raising the intriguing question of how this cytoplasmic complex contributes to the functions of Integrator in the nucleus.

results.subtitle: ## Structure of the dIntS11-CG7044 complex
results.content:
To gain molecular insight into the Drosophila dIntS11-CG7044 association, we co-expressed and purified their complex (Figure 2A). We also co-expressed dIntS9-dIntS11-CG7044 (Figures 1E and 1G) but found that dIntS9 was present at substoichiometric levels after purification even though its expression level was very high (Figure 2B), consistent with the immunoprecipitation data.

Wedetermined the structure of the dIntS11-CG7044 complex at 3.54 A ˚ resolution by cryo-EM (Figures S2A-S2D; Table 1). Most CG7044 and dIntS11 residues could be located with good sidechain density (Figure 2C). The structure reveals that CG7044 primarily forms a large Arm/HEAT domain (Figures 2D-2G), with the pairs of anti-parallel helices arranged in the shape of a horseshoe that wraps around dIntS11 (Figures 2D and 2E). The connection between the two helices in the last repeat is exceptionally long, containing residues 830-920 and forming a ''lasso'' structure (Figure 2C). The C-terminal extension (CTE) of CG7044 beyond the Arm/HEAT domain traverses the open end of the horseshoe, contacting the N-terminal region of CG7044 (Figures 2D and 2F). The dIntS11-CG7044 interface is extensive, with /C24 3,700 A ˚ 2 buried surface area for each protein, consistent with the stability of this complex. The Arm/HEAT domain of CG7044 contributes 1,750 A ˚ 2 to the buried surface area.

results.subtitle: ## The conserved CG7044 DCY motif is captured in the dIntS11 active site
results.content:
The structure unexpectedly reveals that the C terminus of CG7044 is inserted into the active site region of dIntS11 (Figure 3A). The last three residues of CG7044, Asp-Cys-Tyr974 (DCY), are conserved among all known CG7044/BRAT1 homologs (Figure 3B), further emphasizing their importance. This DCY motif resides in a deep pocket at the interface between the dIntS11 metallob -lactamase and b -CASP domains. The side chain of Asp972 is hydrogen-bonded to His392 of dIntS11 (Figure 3C), the general acid for the nuclease reaction. 16,37 The side chain of Cys973 is directly coordinated to both metal ions in the active site, which would not allow the coordination by the scissile phosphate of the RNA substrate. 37 Finally, the carboxylate group at the C terminus of CG7044 has ion-pair interactions with Arg244 in the b -CASP domain. There is no space to accommodate additional amino acid residues following Tyr974 (Figures 3A and 3C).

Based on these observations, the C-terminal residues of CG7044 would directly compete against the RNA substrate. In support of this, the binding mode of DCY extensively overlaps with that of the RNA substrate observed in the structure of CPSF73 (Figure 3D). 37 Overall, the structural observations demonstrate that CG7044 forms a tight complex with dIntS11 and can inhibit its nuclease activity.

results.subtitle: ## dIntS11 is in a semi-open state in complex with CG7044
results.content: We and others have previously established that INTS11 in the ICM alone is in an inactive, closed state. 12,31,34 When we compared the structure of dIntS11 in the CG7044 complex with that in the Drosophila ICM, 34 we found that there is a substantial conformational difference for the b -CASP domain, corresponding to a rotation of 6.3 /C14 relative to the metallob -lactamase domain (Figure 3E). This change is distinct from that for the openclosed transitions of CPSF73 37 and human INTS11, 7,15,34 which has a 17 /C14 rotation for the b -CASP domain (Figure S3A), and does not create a canyon for RNA binding. In the ICM, the binding pocket for the C terminus of CG7044 does not exist due to the closed state of IntS11 (Figures S3B and S3C). Therefore, dIntS11 assumes a new state in the CG7044 complex, and we will refer to it as a semi-open state. In this state, there is no canyon between the metallob -lactamase and b -CASP domains that would allow the RNA substrate to reach the active site (Figures S3D and S3E).

results.subtitle: ## The CG7044 lasso interacts with the b -CASP domain of dIntS11
results.content:
The extended connection between the two helices in the last helical repeat of CG7044 forms a lasso structure, with two helices at the tip of this lasso being projected more than 30 A ˚ away from the body of CG7044 (Figures 2E and 2G). The CG7044 lasso has extensive, predominantly hydrophobic interactions with the b -CASP domain of dIntS11. Residues in the two helices at the tip of the lasso ( a L1 and a L2) contact the ''back'' face of the b -CASP domain (Figures 2E, S4A, and S4B). Most residues in the two helices interacting with dIntS11 are highly conserved among insect CG7044 homologs (Figure S4C). On the other hand, the linkers from these two helices to the Arm/HEAT domain are poorly conserved, suggesting that this structural feature is likely highly dynamic.

There is a significant conformational change for helices a Cand a D of the dIntS11 b -CASP domain in the CG7044 complex (Figure S4D). Compared with the Drosophila ICM structure, the a D helix is disordered in the CG7044 complex, and the a L2 helix of the lasso takes up the position of this helix. The a L1 helix of the lasso clashes with dIntS4 of the ICM, and a segment in the b -CASP domain of dIntS9 in the ICM clashes with CG7044. Therefore, the dIntS11-CG7044 complex is incompatible with the formation of the ICM, indicating that dIntS11 binding to CG7044 is mutually exclusive to its binding to dIntS4/dIntS9.

results.subtitle: ## Structure of the human INTS9-INTS11-BRAT1 complex
results.content:
Our biochemical studies with the Drosophila dIntS11-CG7044 complex suggest that a human INTS11-BRAT1 complex is also likely to exist. While we were able to purify this complex, the expression levels of the two proteins were very low, even though they were co-expressed (Figure 4A). However, when we included

INTS9 in the co-expression, it led to a significant improvement in the expression levels of the INTS9-INTS11-BRAT1 complex (Figure 4B), consistent with pull-down assays (Figure 1F). We determinedthestructure of this ternary INTS9-INTS11-BRAT1 complex at 3.2 A ˚ resolution by cryo-EM (Figures 4C-4E and S2E-S2H; Table 1).

The overall structure of the human INTS11-BRAT1 portion of the ternary complex is similar to that of the Drosophila dIntS11-CG7044 complex (Figure S5A). Human INTS11 is also in a semi-open state, and the BRAT1 C terminus is captured in the active site region of INTS11 with a similar binding mode (Figure 4F). With INTS11 in superposition, a rotation of 4 /C14 is needed to align the structure of BRAT1 with that of CG7044 (Figure S5A), with substantial differences for some of the Arm/HEAT repeats (Figure S5B). The lasso is not present in human BRAT1, as that

loop is much shorter (residues 733-772) and is disordered (Figure 4C). Therefore, the lasso may be a feature unique to CG7044 homologs in insects. Nonetheless, helix a D of the INTS11 b -CASP domain is also disordered in this complex (Figure 4E), suggesting that the disordering of this helix is a consequence of the binding of BRAT1/CG7044 rather than the presence of the lasso.

results.subtitle: ## INTS9 has weaker interactions with BRAT1
results.content:
INTS9 is bound to the side of BRAT1 and has essentially no direct contact with INTS11 (buried surface area of <60 A ˚ 2 ) in this complex (Figures 4D, 4E, and S5C). The b -CASP domain of INTS9 is located in the interface with BRAT1. By contrast, much of its metallob -lactamase domain is not in the interface (Figure S5C). The INTS9-BRAT1 interface is much less extensive than the INTS11BRAT1 interface, suggesting that the INTS9-BRAT1 complex is less stable. A large, primarily hydrophobic interface patch involves helices a A and a B of the INTS9 b -CASP domain contacting repeats 10 and 11 of BRAT1 (Figure S5D).

Compared with the structure of INTS9 in the human ICM, 31 a large conformational change is observed for helix a A and the neighboring strand b I of the b -CASP domain (Figure S5E). More importantly, the organization of INTS9 and INTS11 in the complex with BRAT1 is incompatible with the observed organization of the ICM. This can be visualized by overlaying the metallob -lactamase domains of INTS11 in the ICM and the INTS9INTS11-BRAT1 complex (Figure 4G; Video S1). In this overlay, there are substantial differences in the position and orientation of INTS9 between the two complexes. INTS9 in the INTS9INTS11-BRAT1 complex has essentially no contacts with INTS11, and it clashes with INTS4 in the ICM. This is supported by our observation that BRAT1 only pulls down INTS11 and INTS9 in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Figure 1F).

We investigated why Drosophila dIntS9 has a weaker association with the dIntS11-CG7044 complex (Figure 2B). We looked at how Drosophila dIntS9 and CG7044 would fit in the observed humanINTS9-BRAT1 interface. Residues in this interface are generally weakly conserved among their homologs. In particular, Ser283 in human INTS9 is replaced by Met282 in Drosophila dIntS9 (Figure S5F), which would clash with CG7044 and destabilize the dIntS9-CG7044 complex. Based on these structural analyses, we generated the S283M single mutant as well as the E280R/ S283M/L287A/R290A quadruple mutant of human INTS9 and found they were not able to disrupt the formation of the ternary complex based on gel filtration (Figure S5G). However, the C-terminal domains (CTDs) of INTS9 and INTS11 are likely still associated in the mutants, 31,34 which would give an apparent ternary complex on gel filtration. We then examined the E280R/S283M/ L287A/R290A sample by cryo-EM and found that the particles look like dIntS11-CG7044 hetero-dimers rather than INTS9INTS11-BRAT1 hetero-trimers (Figure S5H), demonstrating that the mutation has disrupted the INTS9-BRAT1 interaction.

results.subtitle: ## Functional relevance of CG7044/BRAT1-containing complexes
results.content:
To examine the importance of BRAT1/CG7044 in human and Drosophila cells, we reduced its expression using either CRISPR-Cas9 or RNA interference. To that end, we generated

three independent BRAT1 knockout human HCT116 cell lines and confirmed its complete depletion by western blot analysis and indirect immunofluorescence (Figures 5A and 5B). Interestingly, all three clonal lines displayed no overt growth defects but demonstrated reduced levels of both INTS9 and INTS11 proteins with only a marginal impact on other Integrator subunits (Fig-

CG7044 in Drosophila S2 cells also caused co-depletion of dIntS11 but did not overtly affect dIntS9 expression (Figure 5D). These results are consistent with human INTS9 and INTS11 associating with BRAT1, but only dIntS11 forming a stable complex with CG7044. 55

Next, we examined the functional consequences of BRAT1 knockout and found a striking elevation of misprocessed UsnRNAs(Figure 5E), a hallmark of INTS11-depletion phenotype and Integrator misfunction, and consistent with the overall reduction in INTS9/INTS11 accumulation and previous reports 41 (Figure 5A). The BRAT1 knockout lines created an optimal system to re-express BRAT1 or BRAT1 mutant proteins to test for functional rescue. Specifically, we generated BRAT1 constructs that are either wild-type (WT), have the DCY motif changed to alanine (AAA), have the DCY motif removed ( D DCY), or lack the CTE, including the a C1 and a C2 helices ( D CTE). To assess the ability of BRAT1 constructs to rescue the Integrator-depletion phenotype, we utilized a previously described fluorescencebased reporter system where the U7snRNA promoter and coding region are placed upstream of a GFP open reading frame (Figure 5F). 52,56,57 As expected, transfection of this U7-GFP reporter into control HCT116 cells yielded little GFP expression versus a high amount of GFP produced in BRAT1 null cells (Figure 5F, lanes 1 versus 2). When BRAT1-WT is re-expressed in BRAT-null cells, we observed low levels of GFP expression, comparable to control HCT116 cells, indicating a complete rescue of the INTS11-depletion phenotype (Figure 5F, lanes 2 versus 3). By contrast, re-expression of the AAA, D DCY, or D CTE mutant failed to fully restore U7snRNA processing, resulting in GFP production. This indicates that the DCY motif is required for BRAT1 function with INTS11 (Figure 5F). Finally, we also overexpressed INTS11 in BRAT1 knockout cells and found it can almost fully rescue Integrator dysfunction, indicating that destabilization of INTS11 is the major driving factor for the observed reduced Integrator nuclear function (Figure 5G). These data indicate that BRAT1/CG7044 stabilizes INTS11 in the cytoplasm, and the INTS11-BRAT1 complex is required for nuclear Integrator function.

results.subtitle: ## Loss of BRAT1 leads to precocious expression of neurogenesis-driving factors
results.content:
BRAT1 mutations have been attributed to a spectrum of neurological development disorders connected to epilepsy and seizures. 41,58-60 To further study the role of BRAT1 in neural differentiation, we generated syngeneic BRAT1 knockout ( D BRAT1) and control cell lines from human embryonic H7 (WA07) stem cells. Two independent cell lines were generated for both control and D BRAT1 human embryonic stem cell (hESC) lines. D BRAT1 embryonic stem cells (ESCs) do not exhibit growth defects and exhibit normal ESC morphology and pluripotency marker expression (Figure S6A). To examine the potential effect of BRAT1 loss on the generation of interneuron precursors, we further differentiated the ESCs into ventral NOs) (Figures 6A and S6A-S6C). 61 Similar to the HCT116 cells that lacked BRAT1, the D BRAT1 ESCs and NOs both display significant UsnRNA misprocessing, demonstrating that at least at the level of UsnRNA, there is an apparent Integrator deficiency phenotype (Figure 6B).

To determine the impact of BRAT1 depletion on gene expression in hESCs and NOs, we performed RNA sequencing (RNAseq). We found that D BRAT1 hESCs did not distinctly cluster from control hESCs using principal-component analysis (PCA) of the RNA-seq, and consistently, only a limited number of genes exhibited differential expression (Figures S6C and S6D). By contrast, the PCA analysis of the NO RNA-seq data revealed tight clustering of the two D BRAT1 clonal lines and separate from that of control lines (Figure 6C). Further, unlike hESCs, the D BRAT1 neural organoids displayed a much more disrupted transcriptome (Figures 6D and 6E). We validated several of the observed changes using RT-qPCR (Figure S6E). Gene Ontology analysis of the downregulated genes did not identify any processes above the statistical cutoff for significance. By contrast, the upregulated genes were enriched in many pathways involved in neurogenesis, axon formation, and neurodifferentiation (Figure 6F). Further, many top upregulated genes are considered master-regulator transcription factors (DLX1, DLX2, DLX5, and NKX2-1) and are implicated in brain patterning and development. 62-68 Altogether, these data reveal that loss of BRAT1 disrupts gene expression patterns during neural differentiation.

results.subtitle: ## UBE3D may be a ''BRAT1-like'' binding partner for CPSF73
results.content:
Inspired by our observations on the INTS11-BRAT1 complex, we wondered whether the INTS11 paralog, CPSF73, could have a binding partner with a similar interaction mechanism. To explore this possibility, we first used the BRAT1 structure to search against all the human protein structures predicted by AlphaFold2, 69 but failed to identify a structurally similar protein using Dali. 70 We then screened through the list of binding partners of human CPSF73 in the BioGRID database, 71 using AlphaFold-Multimer 72 to predict the structure of its complex with the CPSF73-CPSF100 heterodimer. This led to the identification of a complex between CPSF73 and UBE3D (ubiquitin protein ligase 3D). UBE3D primarily interacts with the metallob -lactamase and b -CASP domains of CPSF73 and has essentially no contacts with CPSF100. A prediction for the CPSF73-UBE3D binary complex produced a similar model (Figures 7A and S7A), as well as another model where there are also some contacts between UBE3D and the CTDs of CPSF73 (Figure S7B). Most interestingly, both models suggest that Cys144 at the tip of a long segment (residues 129-159) that extends far from the body of UBE3Dispositioned in the active site of CPSF73 and can directly coordinate one or both metal ions (Figure 7B). CPSF73 is in a fully open conformation, with a canyon between the

metallob -lactamase and b -CASP domains to accommodate this segment from UBE3D (Figure S7C). Cys144 and the following His145 are conserved among UBE3D homologs, including the yeast homolog Ipa1 (Figure 7C), suggesting their functional importance.

To gain cellular evidence that UBE3D binds CPSF73, we first probed the localization of several CPA factors and UBE3D. As was the case for BRAT1, UBE3D is primarily cytoplasmic, whereas CPSF73 and CPSF100 were more enriched in the nucleus but still demonstrate cytoplasmic localization (Figure 7D). In addition, we verified the importance of that long segment of UBE3Dfor CPSF73 binding. We generated three mutants, deleting residues 131-156 or 135-154 of the segment or replacing the WCCH sequence (Figure 7C) at the tip of the segment with alanines (142-145A). We observed that all UBE3D FLAG-tagged proteins expressed to comparable levels, but all three mutants were found to pull down significantly less HA-CPSF73 (Figure 7E). We co-expressed the yeast Kluyveromyces lactis Ysh1 (CPSF73 homolog), Ydh1 (CPSF100 homolog), Pta1 (symplekin homolog), and Ipa1 in insect cells and successfully purified a complex containing Ysh1 and Ipa1 (Figure S7D). AlphaFold2 prediction of the Ysh1-Ipa1 complex showed similar overall structures and conserved modes of interaction in the active site region (Figures S7E and S7F). We generated equivalent mutations in K. lactis Ipa1 and showed that the mutants could no longer copurify with Ysh1 after co-expression in insect cells (Figure 7F). Altogether, these results indicate that UBE3D associates with only CPSF73 in the CPA machinery and that the long segment is important for the binding.
